narrative.text: The resettlement office occupies a converted warehouse on the industrial edge of Ashenmere — a building that was supposed to be temporary when the refugee program was established and has somehow become permanent. The walls are covered with maps showing refugee distributions across seven provinces. Pinned to the maps are photographs of families — the kind of personal documentation that bureaucrats keep to remind themselves that spreadsheets represent people. Gregor Maric has been working eighteen-hour days for three weeks. He has a proposal. It is ambitious, expensive, and may be the only way to turn a humanitarian crisis into a national asset.

We have approximately fourteen thousand refugees in temporary camps and resettlement housing across the eastern provinces. They are not going home — Morivask is still burning, and the warlords who drove them out are still in power. They are here permanently, whether we like it or not, whether they like it or not. The question is whether they become a permanent underclass — unemployed, marginalized, radicalized — or whether they become Veltrians. I am proposing a twelve-million-₭ integration program: job training in construction, agriculture, and manufacturing; language instruction for adults; a micro-loan program for refugees who want to start businesses; and a path to permanent residency after three years of employment. This is not charity. It is an investment in turning a liability into a workforce. The alternative is camps that become permanent, a generation of stateless children raised on our soil, and a Dravenhollow region that becomes a tinderbox.

Twelve million is significant but not crippling. The economic modeling suggests that integrated refugees would contribute approximately eighteen million in tax revenue and economic activity within five years — assuming the integration works, which is not guaranteed. A more conservative pilot program — five million ₭, focused on the three camps with the highest employable populations — would test the model before committing to full scale. Or we can decline to invest and manage the camps as a humanitarian obligation indefinitely. That is the cheapest option in this year's budget and the most expensive option over a decade.

Maric is proposing to transform a burden into an asset — the kind of vision that made me appoint him in the first place. Vostane is doing her job — finding the fiscally responsible middle path. But 'manage the camps indefinitely' is not a neutral option. It is a slow-motion catastrophe — the creation of a permanent refugee underclass that will radicalize a generation of Dravenni and Morivask children who have known nothing but canvas tents and barbed wire. I have to decide whether integration is an investment worth making, or whether the budget simply cannot bear it. The refugees are not going anywhere. Neither is this decision.

choices.text: "Full program. Twelve million ₭, all seven provinces, every refugee who wants to work. Maric, you run it through Interior — coordinate with Vostane on the micro-loan structure. The resettlement office gets proper funding and permanent status. This is not a temporary program. This is the beginning of Veltria's first comprehensive integration policy. The refugees came here because they had nowhere else to go. We will give them somewhere to stay."

"Pilot program. Five million ₭, three camps, eighteen-month evaluation period. If the integration metrics are positive — employment rates, language acquisition, business formation — we scale to full program in year two. Vostane, design the evaluation framework. Maric, pick the three camps with the best prospects. I want data, not hope, before I commit twelve million."

"The integration program is not feasible at this time. The budget cannot absorb twelve million in new spending, and the political environment is too volatile for a major refugee integration initiative. The camps will continue to receive humanitarian support through existing channels. The refugees are not being abandoned — they are being maintained in accordance with our international obligations. When the budget improves, we revisit."
